questions.question: Naledi Ltd has 600 000 shares in issue that raised R3 000 000. It issues 200 000 new shares at R8,00 each, and on the last day of the year buys back 40 000 shares at R9,00 each. Record both transactions and state the closing number of shares in issue and the closing balance of ordinary share capital.
questions.expected_answer: The issue: 200 000 shares at R8,00 raises R1 600 000 — debit Bank, credit Ordinary Share Capital R1 600 000. The full issue price goes to share capital because no par value shares have no premium account. Share capital is now R4 600 000 for 800 000 shares, an average issue price of R5,75. The buy-back: the company pays 40 000 times R9,00, which is R360 000 — credit Bank. Ordinary Share Capital is debited with the average issue price of the repurchased shares, 40 000 times R5,75, which is R230 000, and Retained Income is debited with the excess of R130 000, because anything paid above the average is a distribution of past profits to the departing shareholder. Closing position: 760 000 shares in issue and ordinary share capital of R4 600 000 less R230 000, which is R4 370 000. The repurchased shares are cancelled and earn no further dividends.

questions.question: Naledi Ltd paid provisional tax of R160 000 in August and R200 000 in February. Net profit before tax is R1 500 000 and the tax rate is 27 percent. It also paid an interim dividend of 30 cents per share on 800 000 shares in October and declared a final dividend of 50 cents per share on 760 000 shares on 28 February. Show the year-end position with SARS and the total dividends for the year.
questions.expected_answer: Income tax for the year is 27 percent of R1 500 000, which is R405 000 — debit Income Tax, credit SARS Income Tax. The provisional payments of R160 000 plus R200 000, R360 000 in total, were debited to the SARS account when paid. The account therefore closes with a credit balance of R405 000 less R360 000, which is R45 000 — a current liability, SARS income tax, still to be paid over. Had the payments exceeded the final charge, the balance would flip to a debit — a current asset, a refund due from SARS. Dividends: the interim dividend is 800 000 times 30 cents, R240 000, declared and paid during the year, so nothing is owing on it. The final dividend is 760 000 times 50 cents, R380 000, declared on the last day and unpaid, so it is credited to Shareholders for Dividends under current liabilities. Total dividends for the year are R620 000, each computed on the shares in issue at its own declaration date — the buy-back reduced the count from 800 000 to 760 000 before the final declaration.

questions.question: Naledi Ltd owes Kopano Bank R800 000 at 10 percent per annum with interest capitalised, and paid instalments of R180 000 during the year. Compute the closing loan balance, and then explain why directors' fees, audit fees and dividends are treated in three different ways in the records even though all three are payments the company makes because of the people connected to it.
questions.expected_answer: The loan: interest of 10 percent of R800 000, R80 000, is added to the loan — debit Interest on Loan, credit Loan — because the contract capitalises it. The instalments reduce the loan: debit Loan, credit Bank R180 000. Closing balance: R800 000 plus R80 000 less R180 000, which is R700 000. The interest is a full expense on the income statement even though no separate interest payment left the bank. The three payments: directors' fees pay for the WORK of managing the company, so they are an operating expense deducted in arriving at net profit. Audit fees pay for the independent check on the directors' stewardship — also an operating expense — and the auditor is appointed by and reports to the shareholders, not the directors, because the audit protects the owners; independence is essential or the report is worthless. Dividends reward OWNERSHIP: they are an appropriation of profit after tax, exist only once the directors declare them in cents per share, and never touch the operating expenses. A person who is both director and shareholder is paid through two separate doors — fees for the work and dividends for the shares.
